kurz: Four return measures, a fully worked model case and the effect of credit leverage, which in the 2026 interest rate environment can raise or lower the return on equity.

bloecke.md:
In economic terms, a let flat resembles a small business more than a savings account. It has revenue, operating costs, a debt ratio and only one customer. Whether it pays its way has to be shown by a calculation before the notary appointment. After that, the all-in cost is fixed, and it is the only variable that can no longer be changed.

Four return measures appear in this calculation. They are often confused, usually to the seller's advantage. The measures differ in which costs are deducted in the numerator and which capital is in the denominator.

bloecke.formel:
Gross rental yield = Annual net basic rent / Purchase price × 100
Price-to-rent ratio = Purchase price / Annual net basic rent
bloecke.erklaerung: The price-to-rent ratio (also called the multiplier, Vervielfältiger) is the reciprocal of the gross rental yield. A factor of 25 corresponds to 4%, a factor of 40 to only 2.5%. Neither figure takes costs into account, so both are only suitable as a criterion for sorting property listings.
bloecke.beispiel: The formula always takes the net basic rent. Calculated with the rent including heating, the yield appears a quarter or more too high. This error is often found in the yield figures stated by vendors.

bloecke.md: The [[Net rental yield|net rental yield]] corrects both sides of the fraction. The non-recoverable running costs are deducted from the numerator, and the incidental purchase costs are added to the denominator. There are official reference values for the cost assumptions. In Section 28, the Second Computation Ordinance (II. BV) sets base values from 2002 for maintenance depending on the age of the building, which have been adjusted to the consumer price index every three years since 2005. Since 1 January 2026, these have been €11.50 (under 22 years), €14.58 (22 to 31 years) or €18.62 (32 years and older) per square metre of living space per year. Under Section 29 II. BV, the rent loss allowance (Mietausfallwagnis) is set at no more than 2% of income. Formally, these rates only apply to price-controlled housing. In practice, they are the usual calculation parameter and more realistic than the zero assumption found in most listing calculations.

bloecke.formel: Net rental yield = (Annual basic rent − Non-recoverable costs) / (Purchase price + Incidental purchase costs) × 100
variablen: maintenance reserve (Erhaltungsrücklage), property manager's fee, rent loss allowance, costs of re-letting

real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer), notary and land register, estate agent's commission; depending on the federal state and whether an estate agent is involved, around 4.5% to just under 12% of the purchase price
bloecke.erklaerung: Only this indicator can be compared with the return on other investments. However, it does not include financing or changes in value.

bloecke.titel: From price-to-rent ratio to return on equity (illustrative calculation)

bloecke.md: Throughout, the table assumes the same cost burden as the model case below (incidental purchase costs 11.57%, non-recoverable costs 21.5% of the basic rent), an equity ratio of 28%, an interest rate on debt of 3.97% and no change in value. In the last column, the current return on equity falls from plus 2.37% to minus 0.12% between a factor of 20 and a factor of 25. The factor rises by a quarter, and the result switches from positive to negative.

## Model case

A flat of 75 square metres, built in 1990, costs €250,000. The net basic rent is €750 a month, that is, €9,000 a year. The gross rental yield is 3.60%, the price-to-rent ratio 27.8. The assumptions are a federal state with 6.5% real estate transfer tax, 1.5% for the notary and land register and 3.57% as a half share of the estate agent's commission. The incidental costs thus amount to €28,925, and the total investment to €278,925. The financing consists of a €200,000 loan at 3.97% effective (ten-year fixed-rate period, offer rate of the mortgage broker Dr. Klein at the beginning of September 2026) with a 2% initial repayment rate. The equity of €78,925 covers the incidental costs and 20% of the purchase price.

bloecke.titel: Annual account for the first year (illustrative calculation, €)
bloecke.unter: After all payments, including the rent loss allowance, €9,000 in basic rent results in a liquidity requirement of around €275 a month, or around €260 if the flat is fully let.

bloecke.md: The maintenance reserve is based on Section 28 II. BV. For the 36-year-old building, €18.62 per square metre has applied since 1 January 2026, which gives around €1,397. The non-recoverable property manager's fee is set at €30 a month, and the rent loss allowance at the 2% from Section 29 II. BV. The tax refund arises because the income from letting and leasing (Einkünfte aus Vermietung und Verpachtung) under Section 21 EStG (Income Tax Act) is negative. €9,000 in rental income minus €7,940 in interest on debt, minus €4,463 in building depreciation and minus €360 in management gives minus €3,763. This loss can be offset against other income. At a marginal tax rate of 42%, which applies from €69,879 of taxable income (Section 32a EStG, as of 2026), that is €1,580. Tax depreciation (AfA) under Section 7(4) EStG is 2% for buildings constructed from 1925 to 2022. It is based only on the building's share including the proportionate incidental costs, here 80% of €278,925. Land is never depreciated.

In the first year, the owner pays in an extra €3,297, while at the same time €4,000 of repayment builds up equity. Overall, wealth thus grows by €703, which is 0.89% on the €78,925 invested, without any increase in value. The repayment itself is not income. It shifts money from the account into the equity in the flat. If you count it as return, your own saving is booked as profit.

variablen: return on the total investment without financing, here net rental yield plus change in value
debt-to-equity ratio, in the model case 200,000 / 78,925 = 2.53
bloecke.erklaerung: Leverage multiplies the difference between the property return and the interest rate; it does not multiply the property return itself. If this difference is negative, every additional euro of debt increases the loss.

bloecke.titel: Return on equity depending on the equity ratio
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation at an interest rate on debt of 3.97%. Leverage amplifies the deviation of the property return from the interest rate, upwards as well as downwards.

bloecke.md:
At 100% equity, each of the two curves equals its property return. Towards the left, that is, with a falling equity ratio, the curves diverge further and further. This effect is called the [[Leverage effect|leverage effect]]. It does not generate any return itself and only amplifies the difference between the property return and the interest rate. At the terms of September 2026, the threshold is a property return of 3.97%. Expressed in the indicators used in listings, the gross rental yield would have to be around 5.64% with the cost burden assumed here for the leverage to pay for itself from current income. That corresponds to a price-to-rent ratio of about 18. Such properties exist, but not in growing large cities and rarely without a renovation backlog or problems with tenants.

A credit-financed purchase is therefore not a mistake in every case. Without an increase in value, however, the calculation does not work out, and that should be said openly instead of being hidden behind a gross yield.

bloecke.titel: Calculation with a change in value
bloecke.md: The house price index of the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) was 0.6% above the same quarter of the previous year in the second quarter of 2026 (after +1.2% in Q1 2026 and +2.6% in Q4 2025). If you take this 0.6% as the change in value, the property return of the model case rises from 2.53% to 3.07%. It is therefore well below the interest rate of 3.97%, so leverage lowers the return on equity to 0.79%. This argues neither for nor against the purchase. It shows how little buffer a calculation with average values has. If the value stays unchanged, the result is negative.

Two routes raise the current return on equity of the model case from −1.11% to roughly zero.

With a 10% price discount, the purchase price falls to €225,000, the incidental costs to €26,033 and the total investment to €251,033. Net rental income stays at €7,063, the net rental yield rises to 2.81% and the return on equity to −0.12%.

With 10% more rent, the basic rent rises from €750 to €825, that is, to €9,900 a year. Net rental income is €7,945, the net rental yield 2.85% and the return on equity +0.01%.

Arithmetically, the two routes are almost equivalent; in practice, they are not. The discount takes effect at the notary appointment and is certain from then on. The rent increase requires a change of tenant or a request for a rent increase under Section 558 BGB (Civil Code). It is limited by the local comparative rent and the cap on rent increases (Kappungsgrenze), in tight markets also by the rent brake (Mietpreisbremse) under Sections 556d et seq. BGB, and only takes effect over years. When buying, only the price can be negotiated.

## Effect of vacancy

The 2% rent loss allowance from Section 29 II. BV is an upper limit for the calculation, not a forecast. A single change of tenant can easily cost two months' rent through vacancy during the search, renovation and possibly estate agent's fees. The debt-to-equity ratio (debt divided by equity) is 2.53 in the model case. Every euro lost therefore has 3.53 times as strong an effect on the return on equity as on the property return.

bloecke.titel: Vacancy and current return on equity (model case)
Two reasoning errors about the tax side
bloecke.md:
The first error is to regard the loss as an advantage. The refund of €1,580 only exists because a loss of €3,763 was incurred. The loss arises because depreciation of €4,463, which costs no money, exceeds the surplus of €700 that remains from the rent after interest and management. The payments for the year nevertheless add up to a deficit. With a purchase intended mainly to save tax, the buyer spends one euro to get 42 cents back.

The second error is to regard the refund as permanent. The annuity remains constant, but the deductible interest portion falls with each instalment, while the non-deductible repayment portion grows. In the model case, the outstanding balance after ten years is around €152,000, and interest in the tenth year around €6,300. With unchanged rent, the loss falls to just under €2,100 and the refund to around €880. The liquidity requirement rises from €3,297 to around €4,000 a year, even though nothing else has changed. Anyone who extrapolates the first years systematically underestimates the need for top-up payments.

For residential buildings where construction starts or the purchase contract is signed between 1 October 2023 and 30 September 2029, Section 7(5a) EStG allows declining-balance depreciation of 5% of the respective residual value. Switching to straight-line AfA is possible. In addition, a special depreciation of up to 5% a year in the first four years is permitted under the conditions of Section 7b EStG. Applied to the depreciable basis of the model case, that would be €11,157 instead of €4,463 in the first year. The tax loss would rise to €10,457 and the refund to €4,392. The deficit in the first year's liquidity calculation would thus fall to €485.

The calculation only shows the effect of the AfA and does not compare two properties. A new building costs considerably more per square metre and rarely achieves a correspondingly higher rent, so its rental yield is lower. Declining-balance AfA shifts the tax burden into the future and does not generate any return itself.

## Location and demand in twenty years

The return on an existing flat depends on two conditions that cannot be bought. In fifteen years' time, someone must still want to live there, and that person must be able to pay the rent. This can be checked using the population and employment forecast for the district, the vacancy rate in the existing stock, the number of building permits as a measure of future supply and the ratio of rent to local household income. Where rent already accounts for a third of disposable income, further rent increases are limited, regardless of what the market would allow.

Two general conditions of 2026 are part of the assessment. Construction prices for residential buildings are around 89% above the 2010 level and rose again by 5.0% year on year in May 2026. The ifo business climate in residential construction stood at minus 22.7 points in August 2026. It has improved from minus 29.0, but remains clearly negative. Little new construction means little additional supply in the medium term, and high replacement costs keep the value of well-maintained existing buildings high. Both support rents in the existing stock, but only in regions with net inward migration.

bloecke.titel: Where high rental yields come from
bloecke.unter: The current yield can only be assessed together with the development of demand.

felder.text: Low factor in regions people are leaving. The yield falls as soon as a change of tenant takes three months, the next tenant pays less and a sale only succeeds below the all-in cost.
A high yield despite inward migration almost always has a reason: renovation backlog, time pressure on a community of heirs, difficult sitting tenants. It rewards work and risk, not capital.
The price level still dates from the low interest rate period; local rents have not caught up.
Factor of 30 to 40 in growing cities. The current yield does not cover the financing; everything depends on an increase in value and on sustaining the top-up payments over the cycle.

bloecke.md:
- Net basic rent according to the tenancy agreement instead of the listing, plus length of tenancy, last increase and any stepped or index-linked rent clause
- Service charge (Hausgeld) statement and budget, split into recoverable and non-recoverable costs, plus the current level of the maintenance reserve
- Minutes of the last three owners' meetings, showing which renovations have been decided and which postponed
- Allocation of the purchase price between building and land, plausibly derived and documented in the purchase contract, because it determines the AfA for decades
- Your own calculation in three variants: expected, with two months' vacancy a year and with the follow-up interest rate after the fixed-rate period ends

mitnehmen: Gross rental yield and price-to-rent ratio only serve as sorting criteria; only the net rental yield, with incidental purchase costs in the denominator and the cost assumptions under Sections 28 and 29 II. BV in the numerator, is comparable.

Leverage multiplies the difference between the property return and the interest rate; at a mortgage rate of 3.97% and the usual cost burden, it only pays for itself from current income below a price-to-rent ratio of about 18.

Repayment reallocates wealth and is not income; the tax refund from the loss under Section 21 EStG only offsets part of this loss and falls each year, because the deductible interest portion gets smaller.
The all-in cost is the only lever that is 100% in the buyer's own hands and takes effect immediately, whereas rent increases are legally limited and take years.
Leverage amplifies the effect of vacancy on the return on equity; in the model case, one month of vacancy a year costs around 0.7 percentage points.

begriffe.text: Annual basic rent less the non-recoverable running costs, divided by the purchase price plus incidental purchase costs. Of the rental yield indicators, it is the only one that is comparable with the return on other investments.

Purchase price divided by annual net basic rent, also called the multiplier (Vervielfältiger). It is the reciprocal of the gross rental yield. A factor of 25 corresponds to 4%, a factor of 40 to only 2.5%.

Effect of debt financing on the return on equity. Compared with the property return, the return on equity rises by the difference between the property return and the interest rate on debt, multiplied by the debt-to-equity ratio. If the difference is negative, it falls accordingly.
Imputed deduction for unrecoverable rent, vacancy and unsuccessful legal action. Under Section 29 II. BV, it amounts to at most 2% of income. It is a calculation parameter, not a forecast.

Amount within the service charge that the community of owners saves for future maintenance. It is not recoverable from tenants. The rates in Section 28 II. BV serve as a yardstick for the calculation; since 2026, they have been €11.50 to €18.62 per square metre per year.

Section 7(4) and (5a) EStG (straight-line and declining-balance building depreciation), gesetze-im-internet.de
Section 21 and Section 32a EStG (income from letting and leasing, income tax scale 2026)
Section 558 and Sections 556d et seq. BGB (rent increase up to the local comparative rent, rent brake)
